$$
$\Delta(\theta)=0\iff\theta=1$ and $\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$. Hence
$$
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\iff\theta<1,\qquad C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),
$$
i.e. $x=0$ is the unique strict minimiser for every imperfectly truthful type and the two technologies are payoff equivalent only at the perfect-truth limit where the refusal probability $x(1-\theta)$ vanishes.

$1-\theta$ and $F$ are decreasing so $w$ is strictly decreasing in the monotone sense,
$w(\theta_{2})<w(\theta_{1})$ for $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$ on the interior, and
$\Delta(\theta_{2})-\Delta(\theta_{1})=p_{1}[w(\theta_{2})-w(\theta_{1})]<0$.
The rent of leniency $G(\theta)=\Delta(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$ is therefore strictly positive on the interior, largest for the least truthful firms and monotone eroded as truthfulness rises, $G(\theta)\downarrow0$ as $\theta\uparrow1$.
In the regular notation $C_{x}>0$ and $C_{\theta x}<0$, so $C$ has decreasing differences and the marginal expected cost of strictness falls with $\theta$.

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta ,x)=0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$
with $x^{*}(1)$ indifferent. Up to the degenerate indifference at the top the firm stays with, and indeed strictly prefers, the lenient technology as long as $1-\theta>0$.
In level terms the lenient auditor dominates the strict one on the whole imperfect interior,
$C(\theta,0)\le C(\theta,1)$ with strict inequality $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ iff $\theta<1$.
That is the economically relevant dominance region: leniency is the cost-minimising choice for every non-perfect type. On the conventional description this is the interior dominance region $0\le\theta<1$, i.e. $\theta<1$, and on the stated discrete support $\{\theta=0,1\}$ it is the strict best response $x^{*}(0)=0$ for the malpractice type with the limiting indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at $\theta=1$.

The $x$-free term $t(\theta)$ drops out. Up to it 
$L(\theta,x)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)$, $C(\theta,x)=t(\theta)+L(\theta,x)$ and on the binary support

$C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)$, $C(\theta,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$,

$\Delta(\theta)=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=(1-\theta)p_{1}F(\theta)=p_{1}w(\theta)$,
$w(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0$, $p_{1}=p(1)>0$, $F>0$.

$\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$, $\Delta(1)=0$, so $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ for every imperfectly truthful type and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$.
Mod $t$, $C(\theta,x)-t(\theta)=w(\theta)g(x)$ with $g(x)=xp(x)\ge0$.
$1-\theta$ and $F$ are decreasing, hence $w$ is strictly decreasing in the monotone sense, $w(\theta_{2})<w(\theta_{1})$ for $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$ on the interior.
Hence $C$ has decreasing differences, the incremental cost of strictness
$\Delta(\theta)=p_{1}w(\theta)$ is strictly decreasing in $\theta$ and $\Delta(\theta)\downarrow0$ as $\theta\uparrow1$. The rent of leniency $G(\theta)=\Delta(\theta)$ is maximal at the least truthful types and is monotone eroded to zero at the refusal-free limit $\theta=1$.

Best reply on $\{0,1\}$:
$x^{*}(\theta)=0$ for $0\le\theta<1$, $x^{*}(1)$ indifferent, $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$. Up to the trivial indifference at the top the best reply is the flat corner $x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$.
In regular smooth notation $C_{x}=w(\theta)[p+xp']>0$ and $C_{\theta x}=[p+xp']w'(\theta)<0$ on $1-\theta>0$, i.e. decreasing differences. The marginal expected cost of strictness falls with $\theta$.

Strict monotone comparative statics:
$C(\theta_{2},x_{1})-C(\theta_{2},x_{0})-[C(\theta_{1},x_{1})-C(\theta_{1},x_{0})]=[w(\theta_{2})-w(\theta_{1})][g(x_{1})-g(x_{0})]<0$ for $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1},x_{1}>x_{0}$.
Hence $x^{*}(\theta)$ is weakly non-decreasing in $\theta$; in the penalty-only specification it is constant at the lenient corner on the interior. The strict monotone decreasing relation
$\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}\Rightarrow x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})$
never occurs on $]0,1[$; the strict monotone decreasing set for $x^{*}$ is empty.

Weak dominance: $C(\theta,0)\le C(\theta,1)$ with strict $<$ iff $\theta<1$. The weak lenient-dominance region is $0\le\theta<1$, conventionally $\theta<1$. On the stated two-point support $\Theta=\{0,1\}$ this is the strict preference $x^{*}(0)=0$ for the malpractice type and degenerate indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at the perfectly truthful limit.

Persistent terminological disagreement in the room remains strict vs weak monotonicity. Some colleagues phrase the weak dominance region $\theta<1$ as “more truthful $\to$ more lenient’’ at the top, others emphasise the empty strict decreasing set and the conventional sorting $x^{*}(\theta)\uparrow$; i.e. higher $\theta$ makes strictness relatively cheaper, $C_{\theta x}<0$, so the model reverses the naive signalling story.

No new primitive information has appeared in round 4; the level comparison uses only monotonicity of $1-\theta$, $F$ and $p_{1}>0$ and does not need differentiability of $t,p,F$ or the implicit function theorem. Smooth sign arguments rely on $p+xp'>0$ which is not assumed. The economically relevant level choice is leniency strictly optimal for every $\theta<1$, with the advantage monotone eroded to zero at $\theta=1$.
